A CI check (docs/parity/check_parity.py, run as a contract gate by scripts/run_all_tests.sh -- locally and in .github/workflows/self-hosted-tests.yml; it ran in sdk-verify.yml until that workflow was retired on 2026-09-16) asserts every ABSENT/PARTIAL row has an owning phase and a named E2E flow and that every row cites evidence, so the roadmap cannot rot silently.
$reauditNote: Every row re-read against main. Line numbers in `evidence` had drifted across most rows and are refreshed here. Three states changed: P21 PARTIAL->PRESENT (the evaluation budget and its 504 shipped), P10 PRESENT->PARTIAL and P17 PRESENT->PARTIAL (both were scored on implementing code alone; neither has a test covering the thing the row actually claims). P22's palette gap is closed and its clause deleted.
source: changelog of a larger decisioning platform, assessed against rulemind-ai @ main

features.name: Datasource management + connection testing
features.evidence: app/connector_fetch.py retrieves a source at decision time, opt-in per connector (config.fetch_at_decision). request_mapping composes the outbound call through templates.resolve_template -- the same templating an action step's url/headers/body use -- and response_mapping reshapes the reply through jsonpath.resolve_jsonpath, the resolver rule conditions already use; neither had a single backend reader before. Transport goes through egress.build_pinned_request (DNS + private-range check, connection pinned to the vetted IP, follow_redirects=False) and reuses connector_probe's URL, auth, classification and redaction helpers so "test connection" and decision time cannot diverge. Retrieval runs in executor._fetch_sources BEFORE variables are computed, because steps run after them. Tenant- and connector-scoped response cache with a clamped TTL; per-attempt timeouts and name resolution both clamped to the remaining evaluation budget and resolution moved off the event loop. Covered by tests/test_connector_fetch.py (46) and tests/test_connector_fetch_refuted.py (29).
features.gap: The fast path (FAST_DECIDE=1) DECLINES rather than implements: fast_decide.fast_path_eligible returns False for any tenant with a fetch-configured connector, so those decisions take the full executor. Deliberate -- fast_decide is sync and called from a threadpool, so a second async transport, cache and fail-closed policy there would be the divergence the decline avoids -- but it does mean fetch and the fast path are mutually exclusive.
features.e2eFlow: author a connector -> test the connection -> use it in a workflow
features.note: PARTIAL -> PRESENT 2026-09-05. The old gap -- "connectors never FETCH" -- is closed, and the fail-open behind it with it: _execute_connector used to answer a source it had never contacted with that connector's sample_payload, which is by construction a healthy approving example, at {"status": "ok"}. Nothing here answers a failed fetch with sample data; the default on failure is review_gate, and an unrecognised on_fetch_failure falls back to the safe value rather than to continue. Three adversarial reviews refuted the first implementation and all three were right -- a connector step nested in a branch or sub-workflow was never fetched and still got sample data, an unmapped empty 200 counted as success, and name resolution sat outside the budget (4013ms measured against a 300ms budget) while blocking the event loop. Those fixes and their tests are in tests/test_connector_fetch_refuted.py.

features.name: p12 / PKCS#12 datasource credentials
features.evidence: app/client_certs.py presents a client certificate on outbound calls, from a PKCS#12 bundle stored on the connector (config.client_cert_p12 + client_cert_passphrase). PKCS#12 rather than a PEM pair because that is what a partner's onboarding pack contains -- one password-protected file holding key, leaf and chain -- and splitting it with openssl first means an operator handling a private key by hand. Wired into connector_fetch._build_request, so the identity rides on the request and reaches httpx as `verify`; server verification is NOT weakened (the context starts from ssl.create_default_context, and there is a test asserting check_hostname and CERT_REQUIRED). Intermediates from the bundle are included, or a partner without the chain cached rejects the handshake with an error that looks like a bad certificate rather than a missing one. Contexts are cached per (tenant, connector, bundle fingerprint): the fingerprint is in the key so a rotation takes effect without a restart, and the tenant is in it because connector ids are seeded identically per tenant. tests/test_client_certs.py (26).
features.e2eFlow: upload a client cert -> connector calls a mutually-authenticated endpoint
features.gap: The bundle is configured through the connector's config rather than through a dedicated upload endpoint with its own RBAC, and there is no expiry warning -- a certificate that lapses surfaces as a handshake failure at decision time rather than as a notice beforehand. mtls.evaluate_client_cert already computes expiry for the inbound direction and is the piece to reuse.
features.note: ABSENT -> PRESENT 2026-09-05. The old gap was '0 hits for p12/PKCS12/.pfx; app/mtls.py:128 is INBOUND client-cert verification' -- correct, and this is the opposite direction. Python's ssl module cannot build a client identity from memory (load_cert_chain reads paths only), so the decrypted PEM touches a 0600 temp file that is unlinked immediately after load and in a `finally`; the key then lives only in the SSLContext. Two of the seven mutations run against this were exactly that leak, and both are caught.

features.name: Outbound webhooks with event-type filters
features.evidence: A first-class subscription entity: `webhook_subscriptions` table (migration 20260905_0025), CRUD at /api/v1/webhook-subscriptions plus a /test endpoint (app/routers/webhook_subscriptions.py), and delivery in app/webhook_dispatch.py. EVENT TYPES are a closed list of 13 (the audit event types the backend already emits, plus the decision lifecycle) so a typo is refused at authoring time rather than stored as a subscription that silently never fires. FILTERS are ANDed {path, operator, value} conditions evaluated through logic.compare -- the operator set the five engines are held to -- and a filter that cannot be evaluated does NOT deliver, because over-delivery of decision data to a third party is the worse failure. Deliveries are HMAC-signed with auth.hmac_signature, the same helper webhooks.py VERIFIES inbound, over the exact bytes sent. Transport goes through egress.build_pinned_request with follow_redirects=False. Covered by tests/test_webhook_dispatch.py (32) and tests/test_webhook_subscriptions_api.py (23), and probed -- not exempted -- in tests/test_tenant_isolation_matrix.py. EMISSION is wired, which is what the e2eFlow actually asks for: storage exposes an audit-listener registry (register_audit_listener) and webhook_dispatch.on_audit_event is registered at startup, so the ten event types that flow through add_audit_event are subscribable without a per-call-site hook. Delivery is fire-and-forget on a daemon thread -- a subscriber is not a dependency of the thing that emitted the event and must not delay or fail it -- and per-subscription delivery health (last_delivery_ok, consecutive_failures) makes a silently failing receiver visible. Decisions emit too, hooked at storage.add_decision -- the documented single place a Decision row is written, and therefore the one hook that cannot miss either the fast path or the executor path. decision.completed fires for every outcome, with decision.rejected / decision.review_required alongside so the common case needs no filter; the applicant payload is deliberately NOT shipped, since a subscription is a standing feed to a third party. tests/test_webhook_emission_e2e.py (20) drives the row's stated flow end to end -- subscribe to decision.rejected with a filter, run a decision, verify the signed payload at a stub receiver -- plus a cross-tenant negative on the DELIVERY path and a wall-clock assertion that a slow subscriber cannot delay the emitter.
features.gap: No durable outbox: a subscriber down for the whole retry window misses that event. The decision and the audit write are unaffected either way -- delivery is deliberately best-effort for the emitter, which is the opposite polarity from connector_fetch and for the opposite reason (a decision NEEDS a connector's answer and merely ANNOUNCES to a subscriber). The decision-WAL dead letter added in the same cycle is the pattern to reuse when durability is wanted.
features.e2eFlow: subscribe to decision.rejected with a filter -> run a policy -> signed payload reaches a stub receiver
features.note: PARTIAL -> PRESENT 2026-09-05. The old gap was 'no subscription model, no event types, no filters' -- all three now exist. Routes require manage_access, not author: a policy_maker can already POST anywhere from an action step, so this is not about reaching the network; a subscription is standing egress configuration that sends workspace decision data to a third party until removed, which belongs with settings and branding.

features.name: Workflow step-through debugger
features.evidence: app/routers/debugger.py: session-based step-through at /api/v1/debug/sessions (POST start, GET snapshot, POST /step, POST /run, DELETE). It REUSES THE REAL EXECUTION PATH -- the whole feature is one executor field, PolicyExecutor.debug_stop_before, checked at depth 0 in _run_steps, which sets the same ctx.status='paused' + paused_at_step the executor already uses for review gates, and resumes through the ordinary execute(resume_from=...). Every step runs simulate=True, so no Decision row, no billable unit, no outbound action, no review task. Snapshots carry the context AS IT STANDS at the stop: variables, rule_results, scorecard_results, variable_errors and the next step. tests/test_debugger.py (25), including test_stepping_reaches_the_same_outcome_as_a_normal_run across three payloads, RBAC across all five roles, tenant isolation on the session dict, and the audit event carrying the actor. UI at apps/web/app/debugger/page.tsx, reachable from the Decision Explorer's 'Step through' action (which deep-links the decision's own payload), which is the e2eFlow end to end.
features.e2eFlow: open a failing execution -> step through it -> inspect per-step state
features.note: ABSENT -> PRESENT 2026-09-05. Building it cost an hour to a bug that was in the TEST, not the feature: the helper defaulted with `payload or {...}`, and an empty payload is falsy, so the parity test compared a sample-seeded debug run against a real production run and reported a divergence that did not exist. Worth recording because the empty payload is the case a debugger exists for -- it is what a broken integration sends -- and `or` silently removed it from the comparison. A second, larger bug was found by looking at the actual screen rather than the green tests: simulate=True forces _source='simulation', which is in _SAMPLE_SEEDING_SOURCES, so the debugger filled every unsupplied field from the connectors' DEMO payloads -- it showed avg_balance=45200 and liveness=98.4 for a payload that contained neither. An operator replaying a rejection would have moved a threshold that was never the problem. Fixed by separating the two things `simulate` conflates (PolicyExecutor.seed_samples_override). The parity test could not catch it because BOTH sides of its comparison were simulate=True runs; it now compares against a genuine simulate=False production run, and the seeding test uses a non-`custom` source because _payloads_by_source overwrites normalized['custom'] unconditionally -- a test written against `custom` passes either way.
features.gap: Sessions are in-process, not a table: they do not survive a restart and do not work behind more than one replica. Deliberate -- a debug session is scratch state whose natural lifetime is shorter than a deploy -- but it means the single instance is load-bearing, the same single-instance assumption the compose `migrate` service relies on. Stepping is depth-0 only: a loop or sub-workflow runs to completion inside one step rather than being steppable itself. And because it runs simulate=True it does not perform decision-time connector fetches (_NO_FETCH_SOURCES), so for a policy whose source opted into fetch_at_decision the debugger sees an unfetched source where production saw a live one -- conservative (it fails closed the way a dead datasource would) but a real difference, and the reason stepping must never be sold as a byte-for-byte replay.

features.name: Modelset
features.evidence: app/modelsets.py + the model_sets table (migration 20260905_0027), CRUD at /api/v1/model-sets, side-by-side comparison at /{id}/compare, and a drift report at /{id}/drift. ROUTING is an ordered member list evaluated by executor.evaluate_condition -- the same expression a BRANCH step takes, because routing between models is the same shape of decision as routing between steps -- first match wins, a member with no condition is the default, and an UNEVALUABLE condition is skipped rather than treated as matching. A `model` step naming a set resolves through it (executor._execute_model), and the step result records which member answered, so a decision made through a set stays explainable after the fact. VERSION PINNING is on a sha256 of the model blob, not on the version column: routers/models.py writes version=1 on every upload and nothing increments it, so a version pin would report 'in sync' against different weights. tests/test_modelsets.py (24), probed -- not exempted -- in tests/test_tenant_isolation_matrix.py.
features.e2eFlow: group models into a versioned set -> route by rule -> compare
features.gap: Comparison runs members in-process one after another (routers/modelsets.py:151-163), and because the loop awaits each execute_model the model pool's second worker is never used. MEASURED 2026-09-23 rather than left as an opinion: 0.8 ms marginal per additional member, 10 members at 14.7 ms p50 against 7.3 ms for one -- the fixed request overhead dominates and the worker keeps the deserialised model, so the serial loop is real and is not worth parallelising for an authoring screen (docs/PERFORMANCE.md). There is also no automatic promotion from a comparison -- picking a winner is a human editing the routing.
features.note: ABSENT -> PRESENT 2026-09-05. Building this found two things about the existing model surface: nothing increments `version` on upload (so the natural pin does not work), and there is NO update endpoint for models at all -- retraining is delete-then-recreate. Both are reflected in the design and the tests rather than worked around silently.

features.name: Nested-key input validation
features.evidence: Nested-key input validation: app/input_schema.py validates the decision payload against what connectors already declare (schema_paths for required nested paths, sample_payload for types), reporting every issue at once with its full path including array indices. Hooked into app/executor.py before any variable computes, so an invalid payload produces no outcome, no Decision row and no billable unit. Gated by engine_config.input_validation (off|warn|enforce, default off); an unreadable mode resolves to enforce. Covered by apps/python-executor/tests/test_nested_input_validation.py (31 tests). Extended 2026-09-05 to the fast path: app/fast_decide.py validates before any variable computes, off the same tenant_catalog entry the executor reads, and raises input_schema.InputValidationError -- the executor's own class -- so /decide answers an identical 422 with FAST_DECIDE on or off. tests/test_fast_path_validation_and_budget_parity.py asserts the two paths return the same issue set, including array indices (bank.salary[1].amount), and that a rejected payload leaves no Decision row on either.
features.gap: The model-predict path (app/routers/models.py) is still flat. core/engine.py's validate_input is also flat, but that is NOT this gap: it validates an unrelated policy["input_schema"], which storage.py only ever persists for model rows (4007/4045/4064) and never onto a policy, and core/engine.py is the no-I/O module shared with the Kotlin, Dart and TS runtimes -- it has no access to connectors or tenant engine_config, which are what the nested schema is derived from.
features.size: days for the remaining model-predict path
features.e2eFlow: submit a nested payload with a missing leaf -> INVALID_INPUT names the path
features.note: Promoted 2026-09-05. The stated e2eFlow -- a nested payload with a missing leaf returns INVALID_INPUT naming the path -- is met on BOTH decision paths and covered by a test that asserts they return the identical issue set. It was PARTIAL because FAST_DECIDE=1 skipped validation entirely, which is the same class of defect as the fail-opens: a performance flag that changed correctness. The residual gap is the model-predict path, which is a different flow from the one this row claims.

features.name: Matrix with dimensions + import
features.evidence: The MATRIX ships as `decision_tables` (app/models.py:792): `inputs` are named dimensions, each bound to a variable and typed; `outputs` are multiple and only the outcome-typed one is constrained, so a price or a limit is expressible; rows state a condition per dimension. `app/decision_tables.py` evaluates with a per-cell trace, and `analyze_decision_table` reports conflicts, GAPS, unreachable and shadowed rows through `mece.analyze_mece`. IMPORT is `app/decision_table_import.py` + POST /api/v1/decision-tables/import (app/routers/rules.py): the workbook is parsed in the BROWSER -- SheetJS is already a web dependency -- and what reaches the API is a grid plus the author's mapping, so no OOXML parser runs on a 512MB API process. `parse_cell` turns spreadsheet notation into conditions (`>= 1000`, `100 - 999`, `gold|silver`, `in [...]`, `*`), column types are inferred from the data, and any cell it cannot read REFUSES the whole import. tests/test_decision_table_import.py (38) + e2e/decision-table-import.spec.ts; UI at apps/web/app/decision-tables/page.tsx.
features.e2eFlow: import a 3-dimension pricing matrix from XLSX -> reference from a rule -> MECE reports gaps
features.gap: One sheet, the first one in the workbook: a workbook with a matrix per tab has to be imported a tab at a time. Import creates or replaces a whole table rather than merging into an existing one, so there is no 'update these 12 rows' path. And the cell grammar is deliberately closed -- regex and cross-column expressions are not accepted, because a spreadsheet cell that needs either is past the point where a matrix is the right shape.
features.note: ABSENT (~4 weeks) -> PARTIAL (days) -> PRESENT, all on 2026-09-05. The row said 'no matrix entity' and called decision tables 'flat row/column with no named dimensions'; `inputs` ARE named dimensions, and the row's own MECE-gap clause was already satisfied by code the row never mentioned. Only import was missing. Building it found a REAL bug in the process: with `field_type` defaulted to 'string', `analyze_decision_table` cannot order the column, so every row came back 'not_analyzable' and the gap analysis reported NOTHING -- on the feature whose selling point is finding the holes in a pricing matrix. Types are now read off the data. Two of the first inference tests passed for the wrong reason (the fixture declared the types it was asserting) and were only caught by a mutation refusing to die.

features.name: Child workflow by alias
features.evidence: Child workflow by alias: app/executor.py _execute_subworkflow resolves config.alias via engine_config.workflow_aliases, supporting both a flat map and an environment-keyed one selected by the parent's status, so promotion does not rewrite parents. Alias wins over ref_id; an unregistered alias never falls back to a stale id; the cycle guard keys on the RESOLVED policy id so two aliases for one policy are one visit; cross-tenant resolution is structurally impossible since the registry and the lookup are both tenant-scoped. app/main.py accepts an alias-only step. Covered by apps/python-executor/tests/test_workflow_alias.py (16 tests).
features.e2eFlow: reference a sub-workflow by alias -> alias resolves at run time

features.name: DLQ / Kafka / exactly-once
features.evidence: THE TRANSACTIONAL OUTBOX is the whole design. app/decision_outbox.py inserts a decision_outbox row in the SAME session as the Decision (storage.add_decision), so the decision and its event commit together or neither does -- closing the window that makes 'write then publish' lose messages and 'publish then write' announce decisions that never existed. Table + migration 20260914_0029, indexed on (sent_at, created_at) because the relay's only hot query is oldest-unsent-first. RELAY: relay_once() produces to Kafka with enable.idempotence + acks=all (so a librdkafka retry cannot duplicate inside the broker) and stamps sent_at ONLY for rows whose delivery report came back clean, after flush() -- stamping first would be at-most-once. Leader-gated on the scheduler, because two relays racing one partition would break the per-tenant ordering the partition key exists to give. CONSUMER: app/decision_consumer.py runs a real consumer group with enable.auto.commit=FALSE and commits offsets after the handler, and deduplicates by atomically claiming the event id in idempotency_records -- reusing the existing (tenant_id, key) unique constraint rather than adding a second table for the same invariant. DLQ: a malformed or unhandleable message is produced to a dead-letter topic and its offset IS committed, so one poison message cannot block its partition forever. Kafka runs in KRaft mode (no ZooKeeper) under the `kafka` compose profile. tests/test_decision_outbox.py (20). VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL BROKER 2026-09-23 -- the 5 delivery tests are skipUnless KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS and had never run: the standing gate reports 'OK (skipped=5)' and 0 skipped LANES, so the whole delivery half of this row was unexercised while the row read PRESENT. With `docker compose --profile kafka up -d kafka` and the variable set: 20 ran, 0 skipped, all passed, including the consumer killed mid-flight -> DLQ -> redelivery-does-not-double-log flow: 13 need no broker, 5 run against a real one, including the row's own e2eFlow and an at-most-once regression test that a mutation initially survived.
features.e2eFlow: kill a consumer mid-flight -> message lands in the DLQ -> redelivery does not double-log
features.note: PARTIAL -> PRESENT 2026-09-14. The row was sized at '6+ months for the Kafka half' on the assumption that decision_bus.py would be migrated onto a broker. It would not have been: decision_bus is a 113-line best-effort Redis pub/sub fan-out for the dashboard's SSE feed, with one producer and one consumer and a docstring saying publishing 'is best-effort and never allowed to affect the decision write path'. That is a live view, not delivery -- so P09 was greenfield rather than a migration, which is why it took a session instead of two quarters. decision_log.py:19 had already named the missing piece: 'the durable-outbox follow-up'. SSE fan-out stays on Redis; conflating the two would put a real-time convenience on the durable path.
features.gap: The honest name for this is AT-LEAST-ONCE DELIVERY PLUS IDEMPOTENT CONSUMPTION, not end-to-end exactly-once. Kafka's transactional producer gives exactly-once only for Kafka-to-Kafka read-process-write, because the transaction covers the produce and the offset commit -- both inside Kafka. Postgres cannot join that transaction, so the moment a consumer writes to the database the guarantee becomes 'the effect happens once', which is what the dedupe delivers. Also: the compose broker is a single node, so every replication factor is 1 and min.insync.replicas cannot be raised -- a real deployment needs a replicated transaction state log. And the published event is deliberately a thin projection (ids, outcome, latency), not the decision, because a topic is a wider trust boundary than the database and _decision_to_dict returns DECRYPTED payload and trace.

features.name: ClickHouse / OLAP store
features.evidence: app/archiver.py ClickHouseArchiver, registered in _SINKS, driven by archive_old_decisions at app/scheduler.py:71-95 and scheduled at :409-411. The round-trip is now verified against a REAL ClickHouse container, not a mock: tests/test_archive_sinks_live.py:37,91 (skipUnless CLICKHOUSE_URL; wired into CI as a service container), asserting the exact column list and that `record` round-trips as replayable JSON. Column-level coverage also at tests/test_retention_months.py:418,438. The retention/purge contract is tested in tests/test_decision_archiver.py. Predictor values now reach the same sink: DecisionArchiver gains a DEFAULTED write_predictor_values (a no-op, not an abstractmethod, so NullArchiver and any out-of-tree sink keep working), ClickHouseArchiver writes them to their own narrow table -- one number per predictor per decision would otherwise mean a wide sparse decision row or N rows per decision, and a narrow table is the shape an OLAP scan over a time range wants. Covered by ColdStoreFanOutTest in tests/test_predictors_api.py.
features.gap: S3Archiver does not implement write_predictor_values, so a workspace on the S3 sink gets decisions archived but not predictor values -- it inherits the defaulted no-op rather than failing, which is the intended degradation but is worth naming.
features.e2eFlow: retention job archives decisions -> ClickHouse round-trip verified
features.note: PARTIAL -> PRESENT 2026-09-05, in two steps, and the note lagged the second one. The 2026-09-04 re-audit demoted this row because nothing verified the round-trip; b017dab answered that with a live ClickHouse container (tests/test_archive_sinks_live.py, wired into CI as a service). What was then left was the row's other clause -- it archived decisions but not predictor values -- and P20's cold-store fan-out closed it. The note kept saying 'still PARTIAL' after the state had already flipped to PRESENT, which is the specific failure this file warns about: a row that argues with itself is worse than one that is merely out of date, because both halves look authoritative.

features.name: Canary deployment with delays
features.evidence: app/champion_challenger.py: explicit champion/challenger roles (identify_roles), a traffic ramp schedule (current_ramp_weight over ramp: [{day, weight}, ...]), guardrail metrics (evaluate_guardrails over minApprovalRate/maxRejectRate/maxAvgLatencyMs/maxApprovalRateDropPct), significance testing (two_proportion_pvalue) and an automated promote/rollback/hold recommendation. Surfaced through app/analytics.py, and it GATES promotion: app/routers/experiments.py refuses to promote a challenger the analysis does not recommend unless forced. The ramp drives live traffic as of 2026-09-05 -- app/experiments.py resolves each variant's current weight from the schedule and gives the champion the remainder -- covered by tests/test_champion_challenger.py and tests/test_canary_ramp_assignment.py (14). Auto-rollback closes the last piece: scheduler.auto_rollback_experiments halts a running experiment whose challenger has BREACHED ITS GUARDRAILS -- not one that is merely losing, since recommend_action returns 'rollback' for a negative lift too and acting on that would stop experiments for doing exactly what experiments are for. Stopping is what removes it from live traffic: resolve_experiment_assignment selects status == 'running', so a stopped experiment stops receiving traffic on the next decision and the champion serves 100% because it is what remains. Leader-gated, audited with the breached guardrail (which also feeds the outbound webhook stream), and OFF by default behind EXPERIMENT_AUTO_ROLLBACK -- an automated halt is right and a surprising thing to inherit silently on upgrade. tests/test_experiment_auto_rollback.py (12).
features.e2eFlow: promote at 5% canary -> watch the metric -> auto-rollback on SLO breach
features.gap: Rollback halts the experiment rather than reverting a promoted policy: the canary shape here is a running experiment, so stopping it IS the revert. A policy already promoted to prod is a separate lifecycle and is not touched.
features.note: Re-audited 2026-09-05, ABSENT -> PARTIAL, and the audit found a live bug rather than just mis-sizing. current_ramp_weight was called only from analytics.py, so assign_variant used the STATIC weight: a canary configured to ramp 10% -> 25% -> 50% served 10% forever while the dashboard rendered the schedule as though it were in effect. Fixed; see the commit for why ramping the challenger alone changes nothing without the champion taking the remainder.

features.name: Feature factory
features.evidence: All three e2eFlow clauses, and two of them predate this work. DEFINE A DERIVED FEATURE: app/executor.py:803 calls sandbox.execute_variable(code, source_payload, values) where `values` is the accumulated map of already-computed variables, so a variable that reads other variables IS a derived feature -- exercised directly in tests/test_predictor_backfill.py. USE IT IN A SCORECARD: scorecards bin on variable_id, the ordinary path. BACKFILL IT: predictors.backfill + POST /api/v1/predictors/{id}/backfill replays historical decisions through `extract`, which already mapped one decision to one value. Idempotent by decision id (storage.predictor_covered_decision_ids), bounded per call at MAX_BACKFILL_DECISIONS, and each value is stamped with the DECISION's timestamp rather than now. tests/test_predictor_backfill.py (12), all six mutations fatal.
features.e2eFlow: define a derived feature -> backfill it -> use it in a scorecard
features.gap: There is no separate feature STORE: a derived feature is a variable, computed on the decision path, and what is persisted per decision is the predictor observation. That is the right shape for monitoring and for backfilling a baseline, and the wrong one for training-set assembly -- 'give me these 40 features for these 100k applications as of last March' is still a query over decisions, not a served feature table. Backfill also pages from the most recent decision backwards, so covering a long history means repeated calls.
features.note: ABSENT (multi-month) -> PRESENT 2026-09-05. The row said 'no derived-feature pipeline, no backfill, and no feature store'; the first was already false and the third is a shape decision rather than a missing feature. Backfill was the real gap, and it was hurting SHIPPED P20 too: predictors.observe runs on the decision path, so a predictor created today had an empty 30-day baseline -- a drift report with nothing to compare against, on a feature whose whole job is comparison. The difficulty is the timestamp: PredictorValue.created_at defaults to now, and a backfill that accepts that drops the entire replayed history into the current window, so the report compares today against today and reports NO DRIFT. A wrong baseline is worse than an empty one. Note `add_decision` ignores a caller-supplied created_at by design -- backdating a decision would let a caller reorder the audit chronology -- so the tests backdate rows directly instead of relaxing that.

features.name: Monaco / embedded code editor
features.evidence: CodeMirror 6 editor at apps/web/src/v3/editor/PythonCodeEditor.tsx, replacing the plain textarea in apps/web/src/v3/pages/VariablesPage.tsx: Python syntax highlighting themed from the app's own tokens (light and dark), bracket closing, history, indent-with-tab, and RuleMind-AWARE completion built from live page state -- apps/web/src/v3/editor/rulemind-completion.ts offers the selected source's sample_payload keys after `payload.`, the workspace's other variables after `variables.`, and the @variable(source=...) decorator and its three parameters. Covered by test/rulemind-completion.test.ts (19 tests) and end-to-end by e2e/rulemind-v3.spec.ts, which types into the editor and reads back its theme. Inline diagnostics are wired: POST /api/v1/variables/lint reuses sandbox.validate_source -- the exact function the sandbox calls before executing anything -- so a marker is not an approximation of the rule, it IS the rule. Checking in the browser would have meant a Python parser in JavaScript AND a second copy of the import/attribute policy, and a linter that disagrees with the runtime is worse than none because the author learns to ignore it. The editor renders them through @codemirror/lint with a 600ms debounce (each run is a round trip, and a marker appearing mid-identifier is noise); a failed lint request shows nothing rather than an error banner. A syntax error carries its line; a POLICY violation carries none and spans the document, because validate_source raises on an AST walk without the node position and marking line 1 would point at the wrong line. Linting never EXECUTES -- there is a test that an infinite loop lints instantly and one that a file-writing body leaves no file. tests/test_variable_lint.py (10).
features.e2eFlow: edit a Python variable with highlighting and RuleMind-aware completion
features.gap: The editor is still only on the variables page; the API console and the other textareas are unchanged. Diagnostics are syntax and sandbox-policy errors only -- there is no name resolution, so a typo'd variable reference is still found by running the code rather than before it.
features.note: CodeMirror 6, not Monaco, and the row's own gap text counted either. The dashboard deploys as a Render STATIC SITE and must be self-contained: @monaco-editor/react loads Monaco from a CDN at runtime by default, and self-hosting it under Next's static export needs bespoke worker plumbing. Monaco is also ~5MB against ~250KB for what is one editor on one page.

features.name: Journey as a first-class entity
features.evidence: `journeys` table (migration 20260905_0028) + app/models.py Journey: title, category, policy_id, an ORDERED `screens` JSON list, is_locked, is_active, status and a version that tracks CONTENT only. CRUD + lock/unlock/duplicate at /api/v1/journeys (app/routers/journeys.py). LOCK IS NOT THE LIFECYCLE: `status` is the dev/uat/prod promotion every authoring entity has, `is_locked` means 'people are filling this in, the screens must not move under them' -- so a locked journey still promotes and still duplicates, and duplication (unlocked, back in dev) is the intended way to change a live flow. The SDK half already existed and now serves what the workspace authored: app/routers/sdk.py passes active journeys into build_experience_manifest, which translates them into the camelCase shape packages/sdk-flutter/example/lib/state/app_state.dart already reads, falling back to the built-in demo flows for a workspace that has authored none. Web route at apps/web/app/journeys/page.tsx. tests/test_journeys.py (31), probed by tests/test_tenant_isolation_matrix.py, plus e2e/journeys.spec.ts.
features.e2eFlow: create a journey -> lock it -> duplicate it -> run it from an SDK
features.note: ABSENT (3-6 months, 'largest item in the matrix') -> PRESENT 2026-09-05. The row said a journey 'exists only as fixtures in three places that do not share a definition, so there is not even one shape to build a table from'. There was one shape: app/experience_studio.py defines it, /sdk/v1/experience-manifest serves it, and the Flutter example READS AND RUNS it -- so 'run it from an SDK', one of the row's four e2e clauses, already worked, and the rest needed a table rather than a re-architecture. Building it found a live trap: journey ids are slugified titles, so a workspace naming a journey 'Instant Personal Loan' gets the same id as a built-in demo and inherited five demo SCENARIOS whose prefilled payloads answer screens its journey does not have. Filtering scenarios by surviving journeyId looked careful and was exactly wrong; they are dropped wholesale once a workspace has its own journeys.
features.gap: Screens are authored as a list of {id, type, title} with a free-form `fields` array; there is no per-field editor in the web UI yet, so a rich form is still authored as JSON. Journeys are not versioned as SNAPSHOTS -- `version` increments but old versions are not retained, so 'render exactly what this respondent saw' is not answerable after an edit; locking is the mitigation, not a substitute. And a journey carries no lifecycle promotion of its own beyond the status field: it is not part of the bundle `promote_policy` moves.

features.name: Partitioning / cold storage / retention in months
features.evidence: Retention in calendar months: app/models.py:621 audit_retention_months (nullable -- NULL means the workspace never set months and audit_retention_days stays authoritative, so no tenant's purge date moved), app/archiver.py:72 normalize_retention_months and :113 resolution, exposed at app/routers/governance.py:48,98, migration 20260904_0022. 32 tests in tests/test_retention_months.py. Days remain settable at app/routers/governance.py:37,67-68. S3/Parquet cold-storage sink exists (app/archiver.py S3Archiver, round-tripped against MinIO in tests/test_archive_sinks_live.py); table partitioning does not. The stated e2eFlow is now covered end to end rather than only at the cutoff maths: tests/test_retention_archive_purge.py (13) drives storage.archive_and_purge_decisions and the scheduled job -- old decisions reach the sink and leave the hot DB, recent ones stay, the boundary row is retained (the comparison is strict, erring toward keeping data the workspace was promised), it pages past one batch, and one workspace's retention never touches another's. The ordering guarantee has its own cases: a failing sink purges NOTHING, and a sink failing midway leaves exactly the un-archived rows behind for the next run. Also pins the trap that disabling retention is `audit_retention_days: 0` and NOT null -- update_settings ignores None (PATCH semantics), so writing null leaves the 90-day default in place and silently does the opposite of what the operator intended.
features.gap: Table partitioning is still absent, and it is an OPTIMISATION rather than the capability this row names: archive-then-purge already bounds the hot table by the retention window, so partitioning would make the purge cheaper (DROP PARTITION instead of DELETE) rather than make anything newly possible. Cold storage is covered by the S3 and ClickHouse sinks.
features.e2eFlow: set retention in months -> old decisions archive then purge
features.note: PARTIAL -> PRESENT 2026-09-05. The row's e2eFlow -- set retention in months, old decisions archive then purge -- is met and now has a covering test; the residual partitioning item is a performance technique, which is the same shape of mis-scoring found on P19 (a row scored on a NAME rather than on the capability).

features.name: Rate limiting on resource APIs
features.evidence: Per-resource-class rate limiting: app/rate_limit.py classify() maps method+path to decision/read/write/ai/export/admin/unclassified with whole-segment matching, check_request() enforces the class bucket then the tenant aggregate, and request_cost() charges bulk endpoints from Content-Length. app/middleware.py calls check_request(). RateLimit-Scope names the binding budget. Covered by apps/python-executor/tests/test_per_resource_rate_limits.py (40 tests). Pre-auth IP-keyed budgets and login lockout in app/middleware.py (check_pre_auth_rate_limit) cover the unauthenticated surface.
features.gap: Class shares are configured per tenant/env, not per individual resource id; a single hot policy cannot be throttled independently of its class.
features.e2eFlow: exceed a per-resource limit -> 429 with RateLimit-* headers

features.name: Superflows
features.evidence: Ships under the name SUB-WORKFLOW. app/executor.py handles a `workflow` step, resolving it by raw ref_id or by a per-tenant alias (_resolve_workflow_alias, registry in engine_config.workflow_aliases), loading the sub-policy scoped to the tenant and running its steps at depth+1, with cycle detection on the RESOLVED id so two aliases for one policy cannot smuggle A->B->A back in. The composing thing is itself a policy, so it carries the whole policy lifecycle: app/routers/policies.py promote_policy (dev/uat/prod) imposes no step-type restriction, and versioning and audit come with it. Exposed as a first-class builder primitive at apps/web/app/workflow-builder/page.tsx ({type: "workflow", label: "Sub-workflow"}). Covered by tests/test_workflow.py, test_workflow_alias.py, test_workflow_engine.py and test_workflow_loops.py.
features.e2eFlow: compose workflows into a superflow with its own lifecycle
features.note: Re-audited 2026-09-05, ABSENT -> PRESENT. The row was scored on a name: zero case-insensitive hits for "superflow". Its stated e2eFlow -- compose workflows into a superflow with its own lifecycle -- is met today. NOT marked CUT: CUT in this file means deliberately not built (P14 SQL editor, which has no underlying datasource). Here the capability ships; only the other platform's word for it is missing. This removed a 3-6 month phase-7 item that did not exist.

features.name: Predictor entity + values + reports
features.evidence: A real entity: `predictors` + `predictor_values` tables (migration 20260905_0026), CRUD at /api/v1/predictors, and the drift report at /api/v1/predictors/{id}/drift. A predictor POINTS at a number a decision already produces (a scorecard score, a computed variable, or the outcome as an ordinal so approval RATE drifts through the same machinery) rather than computing one -- the scorecard, model and variable code already do that, and a predictor that recomputed would be a second implementation to keep in agreement. Values are captured at storage.add_decision, the one place a Decision row is written, so the series cannot cover only the fast path or only the executor path. Drift is PSI (app/drift.py) with the industry-conventional 0.10/0.25 bands, quantile bins taken from the baseline so periods stay comparable, and per-bin contributions returned so the report says WHERE the population moved rather than only that it did. tests/test_drift.py (18) + tests/test_predictors_api.py (38).
features.gap: S3 is the only sink that does not receive predictor values (see P10); ClickHouse does. The hot copy in the primary DB remains what the drift report reads -- the fan-out is for long-horizon analysis, deliberately a copy and not a move.
features.e2eFlow: define a predictor -> values land in ClickHouse -> the report shows drift
features.note: PARTIAL -> PRESENT 2026-09-05. The old evidence was that 'predictor' was only a synonym for scorecard in an AI prompt: no model, no values store, no reports. All three now exist and the stated flow -- define a predictor, values accumulate, the report shows drift -- has a test that is that sentence.
